note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in FL.json, gathered 2026-10-04.

byways.name: A1A Scenic and Historic Coastal Byway

facts.fact: The 72-mile corridor runs from the Volusia/Flagler County line to the St. Johns/Duval County line; it was named a National Scenic Byway in 2002 and Florida's second All-American Road in 2021.
The byway grew out of three late-1990s Florida Scenic Highways: A1A Ocean Shore (south Flagler County), A1A River to Sea Trail (north Flagler County), and Scenic and Historic A1A (St. Johns County).
The 72 miles are mostly two-lane road, ending at Gamble Rogers Memorial Park on Flagler Beach, a park named for a folk hero.
State designation date: January 17, 2002.

The highway runs from Mile Marker 110, north of the Jewfish Creek Bridge, to Mile Marker 0 in Old Town Key West, and the designated corridor extends five miles into the water on each side of the road.
It is billed as Florida's first All-American Road and is managed by the Florida Keys Scenic Corridor Alliance.
110 miles across 43 keys; state designation June 22, 2001; Key deer, manatees and green sea turtles are among the endangered wildlife along the route.
About 220 miles long, divided into a Coastal Trail and a Forest Trail, with a recommended minimum of two days to drive it.

Designated November 14, 2006; spurs run south on CR 59 to the St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge and Lighthouse and out to St. George Island State Park, and the route includes Apalachicola, Carrabelle, Panacea and Sopchoppy.
The region is home to more than 300 bird species and about 30 species of carnivorous plants.
National Scenic Byway designation came in 2009.
123 miles in all: a 60-mile backbone on SR 40 from Silver Springs to I-95, plus a 56-mile series of loops and spurs; state designation April 9, 2008, national designation 2009.
The route circles the Big Scrub, described as the largest continuous sand pine forest remaining in Florida, formed on ancient sand dunes.
Florida black bears reach their highest population density in this region and are often seen close to the road.

byways.name: Indian River Lagoon National Scenic Byway

facts.fact: 233 miles; state designation June 13, 2000, National Scenic Byway 2002.
The route passes Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, Canaveral National Seashore and the Archie Carr National Wildlife Refuge, close to the Kennedy Space Center.
The byway follows US 1 on the mainland (Titusville, Cocoa, Melbourne, Sebastian) and A1A on the barrier island (Cocoa Beach, Melbourne Beach, Wabasso Beach), joined by several causeways.
A 34-mile double loop with access to North Peninsula, Bulow Creek and Tomoka state parks, and past The Casements, John D. Rockefeller's winter residence.
Stretches of North Beach Street, Old Dixie Highway and Walter Boardman Lane run under a tree canopy.
Right whales migrate off the coast from December to April, and sea turtles nest on the beach from May to September.
State designation July 9, 2007; National Scenic Byway 2009.
156 miles; state designation March 12, 2009, National Scenic Byway 2021.
The Timucua called the St. Johns River 'Welaka', meaning 'River of Lakes', which gives the corridor its name.
Springs along the route include Blue Spring State Park, where manatees gather in winter, and DeLeon Springs, where a pancake restaurant occupies the old mill house.
A 24-mile corridor in Walton County, designated April 9, 2008, with National Scenic Byway designation in 2021; the Friends of Scenic 30A site is listed as the official byway website.
The route passes rare coastal dune lakes and the white-picket-fence cottages of Seaside.
30A is a two-lane road; Grayton Beach was the area's first community and in 1913 its first resort; the 19-mile paved Timpoochee Trail runs parallel to the Gulf.
CR 30A follows the shoreline through Grayton Beach and Seaside and crosses parts of Point Washington State Forest and Deer Lake State Park before rejoining US 98 near Inlet Beach.
39.7 miles, designated July 26, 2016; the route starts in Fernandina Beach on Amelia Island and ends past Jacksonville Beach at SR 202 near the Duval/St. Johns County line.
The Mayport Ferry carries the byway across the St. Johns River to the commercial fishing village of Mayport.
Fernandina Beach is described as the only U.S. city to have flown eight national flags and has more than 400 historic sites.
A 2.8-mile segment of SR 789 (Gulf Drive), designated April 17, 2001, running from the Longboat Pass Bridge north through the City of Bradenton Beach.
The corridor is landscaped for walking and biking, with beaches, picnic areas, boat ramps and scenic vistas along it.
About 32 miles of SR A1A from the Palm Beach/Broward line to the Miami-Dade/Broward line, designated July 20, 2009.

Historic sites along the corridor include the Barefoot Mailman statue and Hillsboro Lighthouse in Hillsboro Beach, Indian Mound Park in Pompano Beach, the State Underwater Archaeological Preserve at Lauderdale-By-The-Sea, and the Bonnet House in Fort Lauderdale.
The road passes through nine beach communities, with sea turtle nests and native dune plants along the beaches.
The Tampa Bay Regional Planning Council is the corridor management entity and staffs the Courtney Campbell Scenic Highway Corridor Advisory Committee.
The causeway opened in 1934 as the toll Davis Causeway, built by dredging-company owner Ben T. Davis, and was renamed in 1948 for Courtney W. Campbell.
It runs about 9.9 miles across Old Tampa Bay, low to the water and lined with palms and mangroves, with two beaches and a recreational trail.
The 10-mile byway runs at sea level along the bay, with a paved multi-use trail beside the road for its entire length; designated May 23, 2005.
45 miles, designated July 19, 2004; its rolling hills make it one of Florida's most popular cycling routes.
The West Orange Trail runs down the center of the byway through downtown Winter Garden, and the Lake Apopka Wildlife Drive opened in 2015.
The northern terminus is at Howey Cross Roads, the junction of Lake County Roads 545 and 561.
35 miles, designated October 5, 2020; centered on Daytona Beach and passing through Ormond Beach, Holly Hill, Daytona Beach Shores, Ponce Inlet and Wilbur-by-the-Sea.
It became Florida's 27th scenic highway after its management plan went to the program's advisory committee on September 1, 2020 and was accepted by FDOT Secretary Kevin J. Thibault.

The byway is made up of three loops (In-Town, Riverside and Oceanside) and ends in the south at Ponce Inlet, where Florida's tallest lighthouse has 203 steps to its gallery; cars can still drive onto the hard-packed sand of Daytona Beach.
The corridor management entity is listed as the Halifax Heritage Byway CME with the River to Sea TPO.

byways.name: Heritage Crossroads: Miles of History Scenic Highway

facts.fact: 98 miles, designated November 19, 2008.
For over 300 years Native American tribes, European colonists and pre-interstate tourists have used the network of roads that make up the byway.
The 'Old Brick Road' segment, completed around 1917, can be hiked, biked or driven and is called one of Florida's first significant roadways.
Its termini are listed as Flagler Beach and Bunnell/Palm Coast, on SR 11, SR 100, US 1 and several Flagler, St. Johns and Volusia county roads.

byways.name: Indian River Lagoon - Treasure Coast Scenic Highway

facts.fact: 42 miles, designated December 14, 2005; A1A runs along the Atlantic on the barrier island and US 1 runs through Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie on the mainland.
The route runs from coastal dunes to the mangrove-covered banks of the Indian River Lagoon.
Along the highway are Florida's first Underwater Archaeological Preserve, a marina and museums; the lagoon is home to more than 4,300 species of plants and animals.
A 3-mile corridor on SR 16, designated April 30, 2010; much of it passes under an oak and magnolia canopy dating mostly to the early 1900s.
The town dates to 1922 and was founded by J.C. Penney; sights include the French Norman architecture of the Penney Retirement Community, a 1920s post office and a bronze statue of J.C. Penney.
The New Hope Community dates to 1923, when Penney experimented with crop farming and African American sharecropper families lived there.
47 miles, designated April 9, 2008; SR 776 forms the spine, running between US 41 near Venice and US 41 near Murdock.
Highlights include the Olde Englewood Village Historic District on Dearborn Street, Lemon Bay Park, the Manasota Key beaches, Myakka State Forest trails and the Boca Grande Lighthouse.
A 12-mile stretch of CR 714 between Allapattah Road and SR 710, locally called 'Martin Grade', shaded by a canopy of hundred-year-old oaks; Keep Martin Beautiful is the parent organization.
Designated January 28, 2015; the Grade began as a logging trail, was used for cattle drives in the early 1900s and became bordered by citrus groves and ranches.
Allapattah Flats Wildlife Management Area lies to the south of the corridor.
Designated June 7, 2001 (FDOT program page gives the length as 45 miles; the Wikipedia list gives 48).
Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings lived and worked at Cross Creek from 1928 to 1953, writing The Yearling there; her cracker-style home is now Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings Historic State Park.
Paynes Prairie Preserve State Park and the historic communities of Micanopy, Rochelle and Evinston are on the corridor, and CR 325 and CR 346 shelter wintering sandhill cranes.
Designated May 28, 2004; runs on SR 64 from 75th Street West to East Bay Drive and connects with the Bradenton Beach Scenic Highway to the south (FDOT page lists 6 miles, the Wikipedia list 4).
'Palma Sola' means 'solitary palm', after an old palm near the beach at Holmes Beach that sailors used as a landmark to find Anna Maria Sound and Palma Sola Bay.
The causeway has picnic areas and native landscaping, with fishing and sailing along its whole length.
11 miles of US 90 along the west side of Escambia Bay, designated April 24, 1998, the earliest designation date on the current list.

The bluffs above Escambia Bay are described as the highest points along Florida's entire coastline; Bay Bluffs Park overlooks the bay, and the bluffs hold clay deposits historically used for brickmaking.

The road passes Chimney Park on Red Bluff, site of the Hyer-Knowles Planing Mill, destroyed on Confederate General Braxton Bragg's orders to keep it from Union hands; the scenic route ends at the eastern terminus of US 90 Alt.
A 62-mile route, designated a Florida Scenic Highway in 2013 (May 2, 2013 per FDOT).
The byway passes farmland, cattle ranches and horse farms, the Withlacoochee River lined with moss-hung cypress, and Lake Panasoffkee.
A 1925 edition of Travelon Magazine called Sumter County the 'storehouse of Florida'.
42 miles, designated August 18, 2006; a four-lane, limited-access toll road run by Florida's Turnpike Enterprise.
The Suncoast Corridor includes the parkway and the parallel Suncoast Trail for non-motorized travel through a greenway.

byways.name: Tamiami Trail - Windows to the Gulf Coast Waters Scenic Highway

facts.fact: 70 miles of US 41 from the Sarasota/Charlotte county line to the Manatee/Hillsborough county line, designated December 19, 2003.
The Tamiami Trail opened in 1928, its completion funded by Barron Gift Collier after the state ran short of money.
The route passes through Palmetto, Bradenton, Sarasota, Venice and North Port.
Extends 38.7 miles along the Lake Wales Ridge from US 27 south of Frostproof to US 17/92 in Haines City; the site is run under the Polk TPO.
Passes through Frostproof, Hillcrest Heights, Babson Park, Highland Park, Lake Wales, Lake of the Hills, Dundee, Lake Hamilton and Haines City, with lakes and citrus fields along the way.
Designated February 16, 2005.

byways.name: William Bartram Scenic and Historic Highway

facts.fact: SR 13 winds along the St. Johns River through pine and palmetto barrens, oak hammocks and swamps under moss-draped trees, running about 17 miles south from the Julington Creek Bridge.
Designated October 31, 2005; naturalist William Bartram tried to establish a plantation on the banks of the St. Johns, and his book Travels described the region in the late 1700s.

The byway begins 9 miles south of Bristol at the national forest boundary on SR 12, follows it almost 4 miles, turns onto SR 379, passes through Sumatra and takes SR 65 south to the southern tip of the forest; total length 32 miles.

The savannahs are open grasslands with scattered longleaf pine and wiregrass, wet much of the year, with pitcher plants, sundews and wild orchids; the route also passes cypress swamps and magnolia bays.
Endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers live along the route, and Prospect Bluffs lies near its southern end.
FHWA's America's Byways lists 1.5 hours as the time to allow.

halifax.summary: The Halifax Heritage Byway is a new designation, not a rename. It is a 35-mile Volusia County byway in three loops (In-Town, Riverside, Oceanside) centered on Daytona Beach, running from Ormond Beach and Holly Hill south to Ponce Inlet, designated October 5, 2020 as Florida's 27th scenic highway. It did not absorb or rename 'A1A River to Sea Trail' or 'A1A Ocean Shore Scenic Highway'. Those were two late-1990s Flagler County scenic highways (A1A Ocean Shore, about 7 miles through Flagler Beach and Beverly Beach in south Flagler; A1A River to Sea Trail, about 12 miles in north Flagler including Marineland) that, together with 'Scenic and Historic A1A' in St. Johns County, became the A1A Scenic and Historic Coastal Byway, which runs from the Volusia/Flagler line north to the Duval line. FHWA's America's Byways still keeps legacy pages for both old names with the Friends of A1A as contact. The 'River to Sea' tag attached to Halifax in some listings refers to the River to Sea TPO (the Volusia/Flagler transportation planning organization) named as part of its management entity, not to the old byway. The Ormond Scenic Loop and Trail (2007) is a separate, older designation in the same Ormond Beach area.
